newsitem.title: BULGARIA: EMBATTLED BULGARIAN SOCIALISTS FACE KEY WEEKEND.
newsitem.headline: EMBATTLED BULGARIAN SOCIALISTS FACE KEY WEEKEND.

text.p: The ruling Socialists enter a crucial weekend of Bulgaria's political and economic turmoil refusing to give in to a chorus of demands for early elections by clowning students, striking workers and an exiled king.

The embattled government faces a 13th day of angry unrest on Saturday before the Sunday swearing-in of president-elect Petar Stoyanov, who says he might offer the Socialists the new ruling mandate denied them by his predecessor Zhelyu Zhelev.

The opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) adamantly opposes any new mandate, demanding general elections soon which the ex-communist Socialists, registering a mere eight percent support in one opinion poll, would be almost certain to lose.

Planned protests on Saturday, fuelled more by fury at 300 percent inflation that has pauperised millions than support for the UDF, include a silent rally by Sofia "mothers and teachers", minority Turks in southeast Bulgaria and students.

Brief strikes are reported daily nationwide, but have been more symbolic than damaging. State-run national television said on Friday evening news that its own staff were joining the unrest to protest against government censorship.

The UDF said on Friday it would give parliament a "few more days" to approve its "Salvation Declaration" calling for elections and a strict monetary regime approved by the IMF, before stepping up the pressure by calling a general strike.

Government officials appeared nervous that the president-elect's inauguration could be a flashpoint for a showdown like the one a week ago, when protesters besieged and ransacked parliament and clashes with police left 196 injured.

Krassimir Premyanov, chairman of the ruling parliamentary group, wrote to Sofia's opposition mayor Stefan Sofianski urging him to keep the peace after he was reported to have given permission for a Sunday protest near the parliament.

"On January 19 the attention of the world will be on Bulgaria's parliament," Premyanov wrote. "We insist that you fulfil your duties in securing order and legality in the capital and the parliament during the president's swearing in."
The former communists said talks with the opposition could be held after Stoyanov becomes president. The opposition is boycotting parliament but says it will attend his inauguration.
Thousands took to the streets of Sofia again on Friday to demonstrate against economic misery and for general elections not constitutionally required for almost another two years.
Ever seeking novel forms of protest, students abseiled down the wall of a university building and one marched in a skeleton costume to represent the "death" of Bulgaria.
One-hour strikes and rallies were reported in 20 other towns. King Simeon II, who fled Bulgaria as a child in 1946 after the communist takeover, joined the clamour for elections.
"We are all witness to what Bulgaria has been turned into by mediocrity, egoism, greed and powerhunger," said Simeon, a Madrid-based business consultant.
Sofia demonstrators on Friday carried portraits of the king, greeted rapturously on his first return to Bulgaria last May, and sang the monarchist-era national anthem.
The opposition calls the government both inept and corrupt.

"Dialogue...is very difficult as there are some people within the Socialist Party for whom to exit the parliament means to be prosecuted, not for political reasons but for criminal actions," Nadezhda Mihailova of the UDF said.
UDF leader Ivan Kostov urged 20,000 protesters in Sofia on Friday to emulate Belgrade's marathon anti-government unrest.
"We should look to our friends in Serbia and see how they manage to achieve a success with their constant protests," he said. "We not going to agree to a second Socialist government."

The Socialists have proposed elections by the end of the year but the UDF wants them sooner. Diplomats said a delay would aid the Socialists, if elections are held after a new IMF accord and reforms began to bear fruit.
The IMF said it would complete stalled talks on a tight monetary regime with a new government as soon as it was formed.

"Bulgaria is in a state of weightlessness. There is no government, no budget, the finance minister is outgoing and the legitimacy of the central bank is becoming dubious," co-manager of Adlon-Discont brokerage house Andrei Pramov told Reuters.
The collapsing lev currency fell to new lows below 700 to the dollar on the interbank market on Friday. Kontinent daily said lev coins were now worth more as scrap metal.
Like the opposition, the IMF is concerned at corruption in the mostly state-run economy. Students appealed on Friday for probes into links between business groups and politicians.
